title: Which berries have the most fiber?

seo.title: Berries with the most fiber: ranking per 100 g
seo.meta_description: Raspberries and blackberries contain much more fiber than blueberries and strawberries. Compare equal weights and a realistic 150 g serving.
seo.search_intent: Find which common berries contain the most fiber

excerpt: Among four common fresh berries, raspberries lead with about 6.5 g fiber per 100 g, followed by blackberries at 5.3 g. Blueberries and strawberries provide about 2.4 and 2.0 g respectively. A 150 g bowl of raspberries therefore approaches 9.8 g fiber.
content_html:
A mixed berry bowl looks like one nutritional category, but its fiber content can change dramatically depending on what fills it. Raspberries and blackberries provide roughly two to three times as much fiber by weight as blueberries or strawberries. That does not make the lower-fiber berries poor choices; it simply gives you a useful distinction when fiber is the specific nutrient you want to increase.

For a fair ranking, the berries below are raw and compared per 100 grams. A realistic 150-gram serving then shows how the difference might look in an actual bowl rather than only on a database screen.

BerryFiber per 100 gFiber per 150 g
Raspberries6.5 g~9.8 g
Blackberries5.3 g~8.0 g
Blueberries2.4 g~3.6 g
Strawberries2.0 g~3.0 g

The raspberry-strawberry gap is 4.5 grams per 100 grams. At a 150-gram serving, that becomes nearly 7 grams of additional fiber, enough to make a noticeable difference in a day's total intake.

Why raspberries and blackberries rank high

Both are aggregate fruits made up of many small drupelets and edible seeds. That structure contains a substantial amount of plant cell-wall material, which contributes to dietary fiber. You can feel some of that difference as the more seed-rich texture of raspberries and blackberries compared with a strawberry.

Fiber is part of the fruit matrix rather than a supplement sprinkled on afterward. It comes packaged with water, natural sugars, acids, vitamins, and plant compounds. Eating the whole fruit preserves that matrix, unlike filtered juice that removes much of the pulp.

The ranking still answers only one nutrition question. Strawberries are rich in vitamin C and water; blueberries offer their own mix of anthocyanins and other phytochemicals. A lower position for fiber is not a lower overall health score.

A cup is not the same weight for every berry

Volume measurements can blur the comparison because a cup of sliced strawberries does not weigh exactly the same as a cup of raspberries or blackberries. Different fruit shapes leave different amounts of air space. Weight is therefore useful for ranking, while your usual bowl size is more useful for planning a meal.

At 150 grams, raspberries approach 10 grams of fiber and blackberries reach about 8 grams. Blueberries and strawberries in the same weight range provide roughly 3–4 grams. A mixed bowl falls between those values depending on the proportions.

Your total diet determines how important that gap is. Someone who already eats beans, vegetables, oatmeal, whole-grain bread, nuts, and seeds can reach a substantial fiber intake without relying on berries. For someone trying to add several grams at breakfast or snack time, raspberries can be an efficient option.

What about frozen berries?

Unsweetened whole frozen berries keep the pulp and seeds where fiber is located, so freezing does not suddenly remove that fiber. Ice crystals can soften the fruit after thawing because cells are physically disrupted, but the structural carbohydrate is still present.

Jam and sweetened fruit spreads are different products. They are cooked, concentrated, and commonly contain added sugar. A tablespoon of jam is a small serving and cannot be compared directly with 100 or 150 grams of fresh fruit. Fruit syrups and fillings differ even more depending on how much actual berry remains.

A smoothie made with whole berries retains more fiber than strained juice, although blending changes the physical structure and can make a large amount easy to drink quickly. If fullness is part of your goal, chewing whole berries may feel different from drinking the same fruit.

If fiber is the specific goal, raspberries and blackberries have a clear advantage among these common berries. A generous bowl can provide a meaningful amount, but price, season, taste, and availability still matter. Frozen berries are a practical way to use the higher-fiber choices outside their fresh season.

Fiber intake adds up across the day. Choosing a higher-fiber berry can move the number, while legumes, vegetables, whole grains, nuts, seeds, and other fruit determine the broader pattern. The ranking is most useful as one tool for variety rather than a rule that excludes blueberries or strawberries.

faq.question: Which common berry has the most fiber?
faq.answer: Raspberries among the four compared here, at about 6.5 g per 100 g.

faq.question: How much fiber is in blackberries?
faq.answer: About 5.3 g per 100 g, or roughly 8 g in a 150 g serving.

faq.question: Are blueberries high in fiber?
faq.answer: They provide about 2.4 g per 100 g—useful, but less than half the amount in raspberries.

faq.question: Does freezing berries remove fiber?
faq.answer: No. Whole unsweetened frozen fruit retains most fiber because fiber is part of the fruit's physical structure.
